title: Lease Term Length / Commencement & Expiration Dates
where_to_look: The dedicated "Term" / "Lease Term" article (often in or near the Recitals, immediately before the Rent or Insurance sections), any "Extended Term" / "Renewal Term" / "Option to Extend" section, and — for existing leases — any First Amendment or extension amendment that restates Section 1/2 commencement and expiration dates.
required: State the Initial Term and every Extended/Renewal Term with explicit, unambiguous calendar commencement and expiration dates (never a bare duration or an open-ended renewal with no stated end date), with the Commencement Date tied to actual delivery of possession/use rather than an assumed or default execution date. Structure the deal as a defined initial term sized to the business's realistic minimum need, paired with one or more express extension/renewal options exercisable at Marmon's election (rather than a single long, inflexible fixed term), so Marmon can walk away or extend on its own timeline.
fallback: Accept the counterparty's proposed commencement/expiration dates and term structure (including a longer flat initial term, or a shorter initial term with renewal options, or an amendment extending an existing term) so long as (a) both the commencement date and the expiration date are stated as explicit calendar dates for every term and every extended/renewal term, and (b) any extension of an existing lease is memorialized in a signed amendment with its own explicit dates before the current term lapses.
escalate_if: A Term or Extended Term provision leaves the expiration date undefined, open-ended, or determined solely by a future contingent event with no outside/backstop date; the lease provides for automatic/perpetual renewal with no cap or notice mechanism; or term dates are inconsistent across sections of the same document/amendment (e.g., recitals vs. a schedule) such that it is unclear which dates actually govern.
flag_if: Term section states only a duration (e.g., "a term of five (5) years") with no explicit calendar commencement and expiration dates
An Extended Term/Renewal Term section has a stated commencement date but no corresponding stated expiration date, or vice versa
Commencement Date is defined by reference to an undefined or unscheduled event (e.g., "substantial completion," "delivery of possession") with no outside date if that event is delayed
A long flat initial term (5+ years) with no renewal/extension option and no early-termination right
A lease extension or renewal is being implemented informally (letter, email, course of conduct) rather than by a signed amendment stating new commencement/expiration dates
Term dates in an amendment or renewal notice do not match term/rent-commencement/insurance dates stated elsewhere in the same document set
preferred_language: Term. The initial term of this Lease ("Initial Term") shall commence on [Commencement Date], being the date on which Landlord delivers actual and exclusive possession of the Premises to Tenant in the condition required under this Lease, and shall expire at 11:59 p.m. on [Expiration Date], unless earlier terminated as provided herein. If the actual date of possession differs from the date anticipated as of execution, Landlord and Tenant shall confirm the actual Commencement Date and the resulting Expiration Date in a written notice or amendment promptly following delivery of possession, and such confirmed dates shall govern for all purposes under this Lease. Tenant shall have the option to extend the term of this Lease for [one (1)/two (2)] additional period(s) of [__] years each (each, an "Extended Term"), exercisable by Tenant delivering written notice to Landlord no later than [180] days prior to expiration of the then-current term. Each Extended Term shall commence immediately upon expiration of the Initial Term or the preceding Extended Term, as applicable, and the parties shall memorialize the specific Commencement Date and Expiration Date of each Extended Term in the notice of extension or a corresponding written amendment. In no event shall the Initial Term or any Extended Term be deemed to have an undefined, indefinite, or open-ended expiration date.
confidence_note: Based on only 4 findings, but spread across 4 different counterparties (Winston Furniture, Providence Properties, FAE Holdings, Creekside SPE) and all independently rated high significance; the direction was mixed (term extended in two deals, contracted-with-optionality in one, clarified in one), so treat the structural asks here — explicit dates and renewal optionality — as the reliable takeaway rather than a single directional target, and treat this rule as provisional given the small sample.

title: Renewal & Extension Options
where_to_look: The Term / Renewal Option / Extension Option section of the lease (commonly titled "Term," "Renewal Option," or "Extension Option"); any Rent or Rent Schedule section cross-referenced by the renewal clause; lease amendments or addenda that extend the term; exercise-of-option notice letters; and cover-page/signature-block renewal-election mechanisms in short-form renewal documents.
required: Tenant retains at least two successive renewal/extension options (e.g., two additional 5-year terms, or multi-year terms sized to the deal), each exercisable by written notice within a clearly defined window (e.g., 90-180 days before expiration), subject only to a standard non-default condition that includes a cure-period carve-out. Base Rent for each extension term either continues at the rate in effect immediately before the extension (no increase) or is subject to a small, pre-fixed escalation (target no more than ~2%) — never reset to an open-ended "fair market rent" or other mechanism determined unilaterally by Landlord.
fallback: A single renewal/extension option (term length matched to the deal, commonly 1-5 years) with a modest, pre-fixed rent escalation of roughly 2-3% over the immediately preceding term's rent — consistent with the ~2% and ~3.2% escalations actually negotiated across these findings — with explicit start/end dates, notice mechanics, and dollar figures spelled out rather than left to a later cross-reference or open negotiation.
escalate_if: Escalate to an attorney regardless of how negotiations are going if: (a) the extension-term rent is tied to open-ended "then-prevailing fair market rent" or any mechanism not fixed/capped in the lease; (b) exercise of the renewal option is subject to Landlord's sole/unfettered discretion or can be refused without cause; (c) the lease is approaching expiration with no renewal/extension provision addressed at all and no confirmed fallback space (the business-continuity risk seen where a term-extension provision was entirely absent from the original instrument); or (d) an amendment recasts term/renewal mechanics purely by cross-reference to an "Original Lease" or other document that has not been located and reviewed.
flag_if: Extension/renewal section is silent, deleted, or replaced with a bare cross-reference to another lease/amendment document that has not been attached or reviewed.
Rent for the extension term is left blank, marked 'TBD,' or tied to 'fair market rent' / 'then-current market rate' with no cap or floor.
Only one renewal option is offered where the base term is short (e.g., 12 months), leaving a thin overall occupancy runway.
Notice window to exercise the option is unusually short (under 60 days), undefined, or missing entirely.
Exercise of the option is conditioned on 'no default' with no cure-period carve-out, giving Landlord a pretext to block renewal.
Rent escalation on renewal exceeds roughly 3-5% per term without a stated cap, or compounds with no ceiling across multiple option periods.

An amendment or addendum extends the term or updates the rent schedule without correspondingly updating all cross-referenced sections (e.g., rent is amended 'per Section 4 of the Original Lease' but the extension-term escalation formula from that original section isn't restated or verified).
preferred_language: Tenant shall have two (2) successive options to extend the Term of this Lease, each for a period of [___] years (each, an "Extension Term"), on the same terms and conditions as the initial Term except as set forth below, by delivering written notice to Landlord not less than ninety (90) days and not more than one hundred eighty (180) days prior to the expiration of the then-current Term, provided that Tenant is not in material default under this Lease beyond any applicable notice and cure period at the time of such exercise. Base Rent during each Extension Term shall be the Base Rent in effect immediately prior to the commencement of such Extension Term, increased by no more than two percent (2%) over the Base Rent in effect during the immediately preceding Term. In no event shall Base Rent for any Extension Term be determined by reference to then-prevailing fair market rent, appraisal, or any other mechanism not fixed by this Lease. Within thirty (30) days after Tenant's exercise notice, Landlord and Tenant shall execute an amendment confirming the new expiration date and adjusted Base Rent, provided that Tenant's timely exercise notice shall be self-effectuating and binding whether or not such confirming amendment is executed.
confidence_note: Based on 7 findings across 7 distinct counterparties (Hannibal Industries, Fort Acquisitions LLC, GLG Properties, W. W. Williams Company, 319 LLC, FAE Holdings, and IWG PLC/Regus) — 5 of 7 rated high significance and the direction is fairly consistent (renewal mechanics get formalized/clarified, and extension-term rent is kept flat or modestly capped rather than reset to market), but the specific fact patterns are heterogeneous (amendment cross-referencing, sequential option exercise, rent-schedule updates, brand-new renewal insertions), so treat the specific numeric thresholds above as directional rather than precisely benchmarked.

title: Base Rent Amount & Escalation
where_to_look: The core rent clause (variously titled "Rent," "Base Rent," "Rent and Term," "Lease Term and Rent/Security Deposit," or "Rent & Service Charge"), any attached rent schedule or Exhibit (e.g., "Exhibit C – Base Rent Schedule"), the summary/cover term-sheet fields (Base Rent, Amount Due at Lease Signature), and — critically — any amendment or renewal section that resets or extends the rent obligation for a new term or expanded premises.
required: Base Rent must be stated as a specific, unambiguous dollar figure per month and per year, expressed identically in both numerals and written (spelled-out) words within the same clause. Any rent applicable to a renewal, extension, or expanded premises must be set out as a complete, dollar-denominated schedule fixed in the lease/amendment itself (not left to later landlord determination). If the lease provides for escalation, the escalation must be capped at a stated, reasonable percentage (or tied to a defined index such as CPI, itself capped) and must require Landlord to give Tenant advance written notice — with its calculation — before any increase takes effect; open-ended or "without further notice" escalation rights should not be accepted.
fallback: Where a hard cap with full transparency cannot be obtained, accept a capped percentage escalation at lease renewal/expiration (the observed market fallback was up to 8%) provided Marmon still secures a written-notice requirement before the increase applies. Similarly, accept rent adjustments tied to a verified change in square footage (using an agreed measurement method) as a reasonable basis for a rent-schedule update, even if the cap/notice language above cannot be added.
escalate_if: Escalate to an attorney if: the redline introduces an uncapped or fully discretionary rent-increase right for Landlord (no percentage ceiling, no formula, and/or "without further notice" language); the current or renewal-term rent figure is blank, left as a placeholder, or otherwise undefined at signature; the numeral and written-word rent amounts conflict and cannot be reconciled from the document (this creates real ambiguity as to the legally controlling amount); or a rent credit/concession is referenced in the text but its dollar amount or mechanics are not actually specified anywhere in the executed document.
flag_if: Spelled-out rent amount in a clause does not match the numeral shown in the same passage
Escalation language includes phrases like "without further notice" or gives Landlord sole discretion to set the increase
No percentage cap or index formula is stated for a rent escalation clause
A renewal/extension/amendment references a new Base Rent or rent schedule but the actual dollar figures are missing, cut off, or left blank
A replaced Exhibit/rent schedule changes total square footage or per-foot rate without correspondingly updating all cross-referenced totals elsewhere in the document
A rent credit, abatement, or concession is mentioned but its amount and application mechanics are not spelled out
Rent increase is tied to added square footage without stating how that footage was measured or verified
preferred_language: Base Rent. Tenant shall pay to Landlord Base Rent in the amount of $[_____] per month ($[_____] per annum), which amount is stated above in both numerals and written words; in the event of any conflict between the numeral and the written amount in this Lease or any amendment hereto, the parties shall promptly execute a written correction, and until corrected the written (spelled-out) amount shall control. Base Rent payable during any renewal, extension, or amended Lease Term shall be set forth as a complete, dollar-denominated schedule agreed by the parties and attached as an Exhibit to this Lease or the applicable amendment, stating the exact monthly and annual Base Rent for each year of such renewal, extension, or amended term. Any escalation of Base Rent during the Lease Term or any renewal or extension shall not exceed [three percent (3%)] per annum (or, if index-based, the increase in the Consumer Price Index for the applicable period, not to exceed [five percent (5%)] per annum), and Landlord shall provide Tenant no less than [sixty (60)] days' prior written notice, including Landlord's calculation of the increase, before any such increase takes effect. If the Premises are expanded, any resulting adjustment to Base Rent shall be calculated using an agreed method of measurement (e.g., the BOMA standard) and set forth in a written amendment executed by both parties before Tenant becomes obligated to pay the adjusted amount.
confidence_note: Based on 8 findings across 8 different counterparties (NAVA, GLG Properties, East End Maker Hub Sponsor, Tommy Surber, FAE Holdings, Creekside SPE, B360 Holdings, and Royal & Sons), all independently flagged high significance — a reasonably solid sample for a core financial term. The direction is consistent in that Base Rent amount/escalation is always heavily negotiated and material, but the specific sub-issue varies across findings (escalation caps and notice, rent credits, schedule resets for renewals or added square footage, and numeral-vs-words drafting mismatches), so this rule synthesizes across several related but distinct fact patterns rather than one single repeated numeric ask.

title: Rent Payment Mechanics (Timing, Proration & Arrears Treatment)
where_to_look: The core Rent / Base Rent payment provision (often titled "Rent," "Rent & Service Charge," or "Payment of Rent"), typically immediately after the Demise/Premises or Term clause; also check any Additional Rent, Service Charge/CAM, or Operating Cost provisions, and the Default/Remedies clause for cross-references that deem those charges "rent" for collection purposes.
required: Rent (and any Additional Rent/service charges) is payable monthly in advance, with no amount due before the Commencement Date, and an express per-diem proration formula for any partial first or last calendar month based on actual days within the Term. If service charges/CAM are deemed "additional rent" for default-remedy purposes, that treatment is expressly conditioned on Landlord giving Tenant written notice of nonpayment and a reasonable cure period (10+ business days) before any default remedy, late charge, or acceleration applies. Tenant retains a right to deduct/set off amounts Landlord does not dispute in writing within a set notice period.
fallback: Accept "no set-off / no demand required" payment language (as landlords commonly insist on) and service charges treated as rent-in-arrears for collection purposes, provided (a) the partial-month proration mechanic is included so billing at commencement/expiration isn't disputed, and (b) some minimal notice-and-cure window survives before default/late-fee remedies attach — even if shorter than the ask above.
escalate_if: Escalate to an attorney if the clause requires rent/service charge paid in full before lease execution or the Commencement Date with no proration mechanism at all, or if "without demand, without deduction" language is combined with automatic default, acceleration, or lien/repossession rights that trigger with zero notice or cure period for a missed payment — i.e., strict-liability default exposure with no off-ramp. Also escalate if payment-timing terms purport to waive statutory set-off/abatement rights beyond what is enforceable in the governing jurisdiction.
flag_if: Rent/charges stated as "due and owing upon execution" with no language prorating a partial first or last month
No per-diem or days-in-month proration formula for partial periods at commencement or expiration
Service charge, CAM, or other additional charges deemed "recoverable as if rent" or "rent in arrears" without any carve-out for notice before default remedies apply
"Without any deductions" and/or "without demand" language appearing together with an automatic/immediate default or acceleration clause (no defined cure period)
No stated grace period before late fees or default triggers on a missed rent or service-charge payment
Rent and service charge/additional rent have inconsistent due dates or payment cadences (e.g., rent in advance, service charge in arrears) creating tracking/compliance risk
preferred_language:
4.1 Payment of Rent. Tenant shall pay Landlord Monthly Base Rent in advance, without prior demand, on the first day of each calendar month during the Term, at the address Landlord designates in writing. No Rent shall be due or payable for any period prior to the Commencement Date. If the Term begins on a day other than the first day of a calendar month, or ends on a day other than the last day of a calendar month, Monthly Base Rent for such beginning or ending month shall be prorated on a per diem basis based on the actual number of days in that month falling within the Term.

4.2 Additional Rent / Service Charges. Any service charge, common area maintenance charge, or other operating cost reimbursement payable by Tenant under this Lease (collectively, "Additional Rent") shall, for collection and default-remedy purposes, be treated as if it were Rent; provided, however, that before exercising any default remedy, assessing any late charge, or accelerating any obligation based on Tenant's failure to pay Rent or Additional Rent when due, Landlord shall give Tenant written notice of such failure, and Tenant shall have not less than ten (10) business days following such notice to cure.

4.3 Set-Off. Tenant shall be entitled to deduct from Rent any amount owed to Tenant by Landlord under this Lease that Landlord does not dispute in writing within fifteen (15) business days after Tenant's written notice of such amount.
confidence_note: Based on only 2 findings, from two different counterparties and covering two different sub-issues (partial-month proration on one hand, service-charge/payment-timing-and-arrears mechanics on the other) — the sample is thin, the two examples don't reinforce a single clear negotiating pattern, and one of them shows Marmon's side accepting landlord-favorable terms (no deduction, no demand, service charge as rent-in-arrears). Treat this rule as especially provisional and revisit once more instances of this topic are found.

title: Security Deposit / Advance Rent Payment Terms
where_to_look: The Security Deposit / Advance Rental clause, usually in or near the Rent article or Tenant's Covenants section; in some (esp. Singapore/APAC-style) leases it is bundled near "Use of Premises" and "Document Charges & Stamp Duty" provisions rather than isolated.
required: Deposit/advance rental sum is held purely as security (never characterized as prepaid rent), is interest-free, and may be applied by Landlord only to cure an uncured, notified Tenant default (with a written itemized deduction statement) — never applied automatically or at Landlord's sole discretion. Balance refundable within 30 days after lease expiration/termination. Deposit amount stated once in numerals with the spelled-out words cross-checked to match exactly. Push for the lowest defensible deposit multiple (e.g., 1-2 months' rent) and confirm the deposit clause does not silently expand Landlord's other remedies (e.g., termination rights) beyond what is separately negotiated.
fallback: Deposit/advance rental accepted as a security fund (not rent), interest-free, refundable within a defined but longer window (30-60 days) after end of term, subject to deduction for uncured Tenant defaults if Landlord provides a written accounting; Landlord's other remedies (including termination) are preserved but must remain separately conditioned on notice-and-cure, not triggered automatically by the deposit clause itself. Numerals and spelled-out amount must be reconciled before signature even if the underlying number is renegotiated downward.
escalate_if: Deposit/advance rent is characterized as non-refundable, forfeited automatically, or treated as liquidated damages regardless of fault; deduction or forfeiture is permitted without notice, an itemized accounting, or any cure opportunity; the clause preserves Landlord's unilateral termination right for "breach" without tying it to a defined notice-and-cure process; or the numeral and spelled-out deposit amounts in the executed document conflict with no controlling provision to resolve the ambiguity (as occurred in one of the source findings, where "Twenty-One Thousand Five Hundred" was left next to a numeral of $28,500.00).
flag_if: Deposit or advance rent described as non-refundable or forfeited automatically upon any breach, with no cure period
Spelled-out (words) deposit amount does not match the numeral amount stated in the same or a cross-referenced clause
No stated timeframe (or an unreasonably long one) for refunding the deposit after lease expiration/termination
Deposit permitted to be applied to routine/current rent rather than held strictly as security for default
Clause is silent on interest where the deposit is sizeable or the term is long
Deposit/advance-rent language is bundled with, or used to backdoor, broader landlord remedies-for-breach or termination rights that have not been independently negotiated
Deduction from the deposit is allowed without a written itemized statement to Tenant
preferred_language: "Security Deposit. Concurrently with execution of this Lease, Tenant has paid to Landlord, and Landlord acknowledges receipt of, a security deposit in the amount of $[AMOUNT] (the "Security Deposit"; in words, [AMOUNT IN WORDS], which words shall control in the event of any conflict with the numeral). The Security Deposit is held by Landlord solely as security for Tenant's performance of its obligations under this Lease and shall not be deemed prepayment of Rent, Additional Rent, or any other charge due hereunder, nor shall Tenant have any right to apply the Security Deposit toward payment of Rent. The Security Deposit shall bear no interest for the benefit of Tenant. Landlord shall not apply any portion of the Security Deposit except (a) following an Event of Default by Tenant that remains uncured after any applicable notice and cure period expressly provided under this Lease, and (b) then only in the amount reasonably necessary to cure such default or compensate Landlord for the resulting loss, accompanied by a written itemized statement delivered to Tenant within ten (10) business days after any such application. Provided Tenant is not then in uncured default under this Lease, Landlord shall return the unapplied balance of the Security Deposit to Tenant within thirty (30) days after the expiration or earlier termination of this Lease. Landlord's rights under this Section are in addition to, and not in lieu of, any other right or remedy available to Landlord under this Lease or at law, and no application or retention of the Security Deposit shall itself constitute a waiver of, or substitute for, Landlord's obligation to comply with the notice-and-cure and termination provisions set forth elsewhere in this Lease."
confidence_note: Based on only 2 findings, both from the same single counterparty (Royal & Sons Investments Pte Ltd), and addressing two different sub-issues (deposit/advance-rent mechanics and remedies in one finding vs. a numeral-vs-words deposit-amount discrepancy in the other) rather than one lever tested repeatedly — treat this rule as provisional and revisit if findings from additional counterparties become available.
matching_clause_names: Rental in Advance / Landlord's Remedies for Breach

title: Operating Expenses / CAM & Tax Pass-Through Scope
where_to_look: The "Operating Expenses" / "Common Area Maintenance" / "Additional Rent" definition section of the lease (often its own defined-terms subsection or exhibit), specifically: (1) the itemized list of includable maintenance/repair/replacement categories, (2) any property/management fee provision, (3) the capital-improvement/law-compliance cost recovery and amortization language, (4) the Operating Expenses exclusions list, and (5) the "Taxes" or "Real Estate Taxes" defined term (sometimes located in the Rent article rather than the Opex section).
required: Operating Expenses defined narrowly, not by an open-ended itemized list of all Building/Park systems: (a) capital expenditures and capital improvements (roof replacement, parking resurfacing, structural/foundation/exterior wall/major Building-system replacement) excluded by default; (b) any management/administrative fee payable to Landlord or a Landlord affiliate capped at 3% of Operating Expenses; (c) capital costs to comply with law includable only when required by a Legal Requirement first enacted or made applicable AFTER the Lease date (never to cure Landlord's pre-existing/legacy non-compliance), amortized over the improvement's full useful life with no artificial short amortization ceiling; (d) a full standard exclusions list carved out of Operating Expenses: Landlord's income/franchise/transfer/estate taxes, capital expenditures, leasing commissions and tenant-improvement costs, debt service/financing costs, salaries/benefits of personnel not dedicated solely to the Building, costs to cure latent defects/Hazardous Substances/pre-existing law violations, fines/penalties from Landlord's own default or negligence, and any duplicate recovery of the same cost; and (e) "Taxes"/"Real Estate Taxes" defined narrowly as ad valorem real property taxes and assessments only, expressly excluding Landlord's income, franchise, transfer, and estate taxes.
fallback: If Landlord resists the full exclusions package, accept a shorter but still substantive exclusions list that at minimum removes Landlord's income-type taxes, capital expenditures/structural replacement costs, and debt-service/financing costs from Operating Expenses, and narrows "Taxes" to real-estate-type taxes. If a hard 3% management-fee cap is not obtainable, accept a cap tied to a stated market-rate ceiling (e.g., a fixed percentage in the mid-single digits) rather than no cap. If full-useful-life amortization for law-compliance capital costs is not obtainable, accept a longer fixed amortization ceiling (e.g., 15 years) rather than reverting to a short (e.g., 10-year) ceiling, and hold firm on excluding compliance costs tied to laws that predate the Lease.
escalate_if: Landlord's draft (i) includes an unbounded, itemized list making Tenant responsible for essentially all Building- and Park-wide capital systems (roof, paving, structural, all mechanical) as Operating Expenses with no capital-expenditure exclusion at all; (ii) imposes a management/administrative fee payable to a Landlord affiliate with no cap whatsoever; (iii) defines "Taxes" as "any tax" or otherwise broadly enough to sweep in Landlord's income/franchise taxes; or (iv) allows Landlord to charge Tenant for capital costs to cure Landlord's own pre-existing legal non-compliance, or refuses to include any Operating Expenses exclusions list at all. Any of these should go to an attorney regardless of how the rest of the negotiation is trending, since they shift open-ended capital and tax risk onto Tenant.
flag_if: Operating Expenses definition contains a long itemized list of specific Building/Park systems (roof, HVAC, paving, structural elements) with no accompanying capital-expenditure exclusion
No percentage or dollar cap on management/administrative fees, especially fees payable to a Landlord affiliate
"Taxes" or "Real Estate Taxes" is defined as "any tax" or is otherwise broad enough to include Landlord's income, franchise, transfer, or estate taxes
Capital improvement / law-compliance cost-recovery language does not distinguish between laws in effect before vs. after the Lease date
No amortization period is specified for capital cost pass-throughs, or an unusually short ceiling (e.g., 5-10 years) front-loads the annual charge to Tenant

Standard exclusions are missing from the Operating Expenses definition (leasing commissions, tenant-improvement costs, debt service, Landlord's income taxes, capital expenditures, latent-defect/Hazardous-Substances remediation, duplicate charges)
Operating Expenses / CAM is defined by an open-ended catch-all (e.g., "all costs of operating the Building") rather than an itemized, exclusion-qualified definition
preferred_language: "Operating Expenses" means the actual, reasonable costs paid or incurred by Landlord in operating, managing, maintaining, and repairing the Building and the Project, determined in accordance with sound accounting principles consistently applied. Operating Expenses shall exclude: (a) Landlord's income, franchise, estate, inheritance, transfer, gift, and gross-receipts taxes, and any tax based on rent, except to the extent such amount would otherwise qualify as Taxes under this Lease; (b) capital expenditures and capital improvements of any kind, including without limitation roof replacement (as distinguished from routine roof repair and maintenance), parking area resurfacing, and repair or replacement of the foundation, floors, exterior walls, roof structure, or other structural or major Building systems, except as expressly permitted under clause (f) below; (c) leasing commissions, marketing costs, and costs of renovating or improving space for tenants or prospective tenants; (d) debt service, ground rent, and other financing or refinancing costs; (e) salaries, wages, and benefits of personnel not dedicated exclusively to the Building or Project; (f) the cost of capital additions or alterations required solely to comply with any Legal Requirement first enacted, or first made applicable to the Building, after the date of this Lease (expressly excluding any cost arising from a Legal Requirement in effect as of the date of this Lease or from Landlord's violation thereof), amortized on a straight-line basis over the full useful life of the improvement as reasonably determined in accordance with sound accounting principles; (g) costs to remediate Hazardous Substances or to cure latent defects or violations of law existing as of the date of this Lease; (h) fines, penalties, and interest resulting from Landlord's negligence, violation of law, or default under any agreement; (i) any management or administrative fee payable to Landlord or any affiliate of Landlord in excess of three percent (3%) of total Operating Expenses (exclusive of such fee) for the applicable calendar year; and (j) any cost otherwise includable in Operating Expenses to the extent Landlord actually receives reimbursement from insurance, warranty, condemnation award, or any third party, or to the extent such cost would otherwise result in Landlord's duplicate recovery of the same cost from Tenant. "Taxes" means real estate ad valorem taxes and assessments levied against the Building and the Project by any governmental authority, and expressly excludes Landlord's income, franchise, capital stock, transfer, estate, and inheritance taxes.
confidence_note: Based on 4 findings, all significance "high" and all pointing the same direction (narrowing Operating Expenses scope, capping the management fee, restricting law-compliance capital pass-throughs, and narrowing "Taxes") - but all 4 come from a single negotiated lease with one counterparty (Indiana Athletic Apparel, LLC, request 3807), not 4 independent deals, so this reflects one well-documented instance rather than a confirmed cross-counterparty market pattern; priority is set to PRESS rather than MUST PRESS on that basis, and this rule should be revisited (and likely upgraded) if the same pattern shows up in other leases.

title: Insurance Coverage & Liability/Damage Allocation
where_to_look: Indemnification clause; Insurance section (Property/Casualty Insurance requirements, often labeled "Property Insurance"); Liability for Damage / Waiver of Subrogation provisions; Alterations, Damage & Tenant-Installations section (damage liability for tenant/agents/contractors and IT/cabling consent rights); and any Lease Amendment or Addendum signed when premises size, use, or occupied space changes, since insurance scope is frequently revisited there.
required: Mutual, negligence-based risk allocation rather than a one-way transfer onto Marmon: (1) reciprocal indemnification — each party indemnifies the other only for claims arising from its own (or its employees'/contractors'/agents') negligence, gross negligence, willful misconduct, or breach, expressly excluding consequential/indirect/punitive damages and excluding matters caused by the indemnified party's own negligence or willful misconduct; (2) property-damage liability allocated on a negligence basis (each party liable only for damage it negligently, recklessly, or intentionally causes to the other's property), paired with a mutual waiver of subrogation and a requirement that both parties carry "Causes of Loss – Special Form" (all-risk) or equivalent property insurance on their respective interests; (3) any insurance-scope expansion tied to Tenant's own added space/use only, not open-ended; (4) alterations/IT-installation consent rights subject to a "not unreasonably withheld" standard rather than the counterparty's unfettered "absolute discretion," with damage liability and installation/removal costs on Tenant limited to damage it or its invitees actually cause.
fallback: Where full mutuality isn't obtainable, accept a one-way indemnity running to the landlord/counterparty provided it is expressly limited to Tenant's (or its employees'/contractors'/agents') negligence, gross negligence, willful misconduct, or breach — not "any and all" claims without qualification — and carved out for the counterparty's own negligence or willful misconduct. Separately, still insist on: a mutual waiver of subrogation and modernized "Special Form"/all-risk (not narrower "Broad Form"/named-perils) property insurance language even if the liability-for-damage clause itself is not made fully mutual; and a reasonableness qualifier on any consent right over alterations/IT installations even if the cost-shifting onto Tenant is retained.
escalate_if: Escalate to an attorney regardless of negotiation posture if: the draft imposes uncapped indemnification with no carve-out for the counterparty's own negligence or willful misconduct; the indemnity or damage-liability language sweeps in consequential, indirect, or punitive damages; Tenant is made liable for pre-existing conditions or the counterparty's building-systems/structural failures; the counterparty retains "sole"/"absolute discretion" to refuse Tenant alterations or IT installations with no reasonableness standard while also shifting unlimited damage liability (including for invitees/visitors) onto Tenant; or the insurance/subrogation-waiver obligation is one-sided (only Tenant waives or only Tenant must carry/expand coverage) with no reciprocal obligation on the counterparty.
flag_if: Indemnification clause obligates Tenant to indemnify the landlord/counterparty but contains no reciprocal indemnity running the other way
Indemnity or damage-liability language uses unqualified 'any and all claims/losses' phrasing with no limitation to negligence, gross negligence, willful misconduct, or breach
No carve-out excluding the counterparty's own negligence or willful misconduct from Tenant's indemnification obligation
Insurance section requires Tenant alone to maintain or expand coverage (e.g., due to added space, inventory, or personnel) with no matching obligation on the landlord/counterparty
Property insurance is described in outdated/narrow named-perils terms ('Broad Form,' 'fire and extended coverage') rather than 'Causes of Loss – Special Form' / all-risk or equivalent
Liability-for-damage clause lacks a mutual waiver-of-subrogation provision paired with the insurance requirement

Alterations/IT-installation clause gives the landlord 'sole' or 'absolute discretion' to withhold consent with no reasonableness standard, while shifting unlimited damage liability (including for agents/contractors/invitees) onto Tenant

Draft is entirely silent on indemnification, liability-for-damage, or insurance scope (common in informal early-stage proposals) — the gap should be flagged and filled on Marmon's terms, not left unaddressed
preferred_language:
Indemnification. Each party (the "Indemnifying Party") shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless the other party and its officers, employees, and agents (the "Indemnified Party") from and against any and all third-party claims, losses, damages, liabilities, and reasonable expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) to the extent arising out of the negligence, gross negligence, willful misconduct, or breach of this Agreement by the Indemnifying Party or its employees, contractors, or agents, except to the extent caused by the negligence or willful misconduct of the Indemnified Party. Neither party's indemnification obligation under this Section shall extend to consequential, indirect, special, or punitive damages.

Insurance and Waiver of Subrogation. Landlord and Tenant shall each, at its own expense, maintain property insurance covering its respective interest in the Premises on a "Causes of Loss – Special Form" (all-risk) basis or its equivalent, in commercially reasonable amounts. Each party's property insurance policy shall include a waiver of subrogation in favor of the other party, and each party hereby waives any right of recovery against the other for damage to its own property to the extent such damage is covered, or required hereunder to be covered, by insurance, regardless of the negligence of the party to be charged.

Liability for Damage. Except as insured or required to be insured under this Section, each party shall be liable to the other for damage to the other's property proximately caused by the negligent, reckless, or intentional acts of that party or its employees, contractors, agents, or invitees.

Alterations; Damage; Installations. Tenant shall be liable for damage to the Premises caused by Tenant or those entering the Premises with Tenant's express or implied permission, including Tenant's employees, contractors, and agents, except to the extent such damage is covered by insurance maintained (or required to be maintained) by Landlord or arises from Landlord's negligence or willful misconduct. Tenant shall not install cabling, IT, or telecommunications connections without Landlord's prior written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed; Tenant shall bear the reasonable cost of installation and removal of any such installations.
confidence_note: Based on only 4 findings, each from a different counterparty and a different contract sub-type (a traditional lease, a lease addendum expanding space, a storage-lease amendment, and a flex-office/coworking license agreement); the direction is fairly consistent — counterparties tend to start from silence or a one-way, tenant-unfavorable risk allocation, with a fully mutual negligence-based standard achieved in only one of the four instances — but the small sample and varied fact patterns make this rule provisional, so priority is set to PRESS rather than MUST PRESS.

title: Default & Cure/Notice Period Mechanics
where_to_look: The lease's "Default," "Events of Default," "Tenant's Default," or "Remedies" section (often a late-added or heavily negotiated section, sometimes with no counterpart in the initial proposal/LOI); also check any clause elsewhere in the lease that conditions Tenant's other rights (access to Premises, renewal/expansion options, subletting/assignment, signage) on Tenant "not being in default" — the exact notice/cure wording used there matters.
required: (1) Every default — including nonpayment of Rent — requires written notice from the non-defaulting party before any remedy may be exercised; no carve-out excusing notice for monetary default. (2) Defined, reasonable cure periods (e.g., 5-10 days for monetary default, 30 days for non-monetary default with diligent-prosecution extension). (3) No landlord self-help remedies — no unilateral lock-changing, lock-out, or seizure of Tenant's property; repossession only through lawful judicial process. (4) No provision purporting to waive, override, or supersede state statutory landlord-tenant notice/eviction protections. (5) Anywhere Tenant's other rights (access, options, etc.) are conditioned on absence of default, the trigger must be default "beyond any applicable notice AND cure period" — not "cure period" alone.
fallback: If a shorter notice-and-cure window is the price of movement, accept it (e.g., 10 days' written notice for monetary default) as long as written notice itself is preserved for every default type — do not trade away the notice requirement to shorten the clock. If Landlord self-help/lock-out language cannot be struck entirely, at minimum condition it on the full notice-and-cure period having already run and add an express savings clause that the Lease supplements rather than overrides state statutory tenant protections. The "notice or cure period" (rather than "cure period" alone) wording for conditioned Tenant rights (access, options, etc.) has been obtained in practice and should be treated as an easily achievable floor.
escalate_if: Escalate to an attorney regardless of how talks are going if the counterparty's draft: (a) allows self-help repossession, lock-changing, or lock-out of the Premises without prior judicial process; (b) states or implies the Lease "supersedes"/"controls over" a state Property Code or other statutory landlord-tenant protection; (c) exempts any default type (especially nonpayment of Rent) from a written-notice requirement; or (d) is entirely silent on default/remedies in an otherwise fully negotiated lease, since such provisions have been observed to be inserted later with landlord-favorable, hard-to-walk-back terms.
flag_if: Text stating a party "shall not be required to provide" written notice for any default (especially nonpayment of Rent)
Language permitting Landlord to "change the door lock(s)", "lock out", or otherwise physically bar access to the Premises
Any reference to the Lease "superseding" or "controlling over" a state Property Code or similar landlord-tenant statute
A brand-new "Default"/"Remedies" section appearing in a later draft with no counterpart in the earlier LOI/proposal
A clause conditioning Tenant's access, options, or other rights on absence of default that references only a "cure period" and omits "notice period"
preferred_language:
10. Default; Notice and Cure.
(a) Monetary Default. If Tenant fails to pay any installment of Rent or other sum due under this Lease when due, and such failure continues for ten (10) days after Landlord delivers written notice thereof to Tenant, Tenant shall be in default under this Lease ("Monetary Default").
(b) Non-Monetary Default. If Tenant fails to perform any other obligation under this Lease, and such failure continues for thirty (30) days after Landlord delivers written notice thereof to Tenant (or, if such default cannot reasonably be cured within thirty (30) days, if Tenant fails to commence cure within such period and thereafter diligently prosecute the same to completion), Tenant shall be in default under this Lease ("Non-Monetary Default").
(c) Remedies. Upon a Monetary Default or Non-Monetary Default that remains uncured beyond the applicable notice and cure period set forth above, Landlord may pursue any remedy available at law or in equity, including termination of this Lease and recovery of possession, but only through lawful judicial process. Landlord shall have no right to employ self-help, to change, add, or disable any lock to the Premises, or otherwise to take possession of the Premises or of Tenant's property except pursuant to a judgment or order of a court of competent jurisdiction. Nothing in this Section shall be construed to waive, limit, or supersede any notice, cure, or procedural protection afforded to either party under applicable law, including the [State] Property Code.
(d) Conditioned Rights. Wherever this Lease conditions Tenant's exercise of any right (including access to the Premises, renewal or expansion options, or assignment/subletting rights) on Tenant not being in default, that condition is satisfied unless Tenant is in default beyond the applicable notice and cure period described in this Section 10.
confidence_note: Based on only 2 findings (1 "Default," 1 "Tenant's Access Rights"), from 2 different counterparties, with mixed signal: the Default finding is high-significance but shows a tenant-adverse outcome (landlord self-help lock-out plus an override of the Texas Property Code inserted with no counterpart in the earlier proposal), while the Tenant's Access Rights finding is medium-significance and shows a modest tenant-favorable notice-wording win — treat this rule as provisional and revisit priority once more findings accumulate.

title: Landlord Reserved Rights (Relocation & Premises Access)
where_to_look: Landlord's/Operator's Reserved Rights or Miscellaneous article of a lease (look for a "Right to Relocate," "Substitution of Premises," or "Landlord's Reserved Rights" clause) and the entry/access provisions of the General Terms and Conditions in flexible-workspace or coworking agreements (look for "Access to the Accommodation," "Right of Entry," or "Hybrid Working" language).
required: No unilateral right for Landlord/Operator to relocate Tenant or to enter for marketing/remarketing purposes at will. If Landlord insists on a relocation right, it must be: entirely at Landlord's sole cost and expense (moving, reinstallation, signage, telecom/data reconnection); to space of substantially equal or greater size and comparable or superior quality, configuration, and location; on not less than 90 days' prior written notice; with Tenant having a right to terminate without penalty if the substitute space is unsuitable, and rent abatement for any resulting downtime. Access/entry rights should be limited to genuine emergencies (no notice) or defined purposes (inspection, repair, showing to prospective purchasers/lenders/tenants) on at least 48 hours' notice, with any "remarket the space" access limited to a defined pre-termination window, and any hybrid-working/shared-use permission tied to an enforceable maximum-occupancy cap.
fallback: Accept a landlord/operator reserved right to relocate or access the premises, but hold the line on the baseline guardrails actually seen in practice: relocation at Landlord's sole cost and expense, to premises "substantially similar" in area and quality, on at least 60 days' prior written notice; and, for flexible-workspace/access clauses, preserve the operator's broad entry/remarketing right but keep a hard, enforceable maximum-occupancy cap on any hybrid-working or shared-use permission.
escalate_if: Escalate to an attorney regardless of how negotiations are trending if: the relocation right contains no cost-shifting to Landlord (i.e., Tenant would bear its own moving/reinstallation costs); there is no "substantially similar" size/quality/configuration standard (Landlord could move Tenant to materially inferior space); notice is silent or under 30 days; the access/entry right permits entry "at any time" for non-emergency purposes with no notice requirement at all; or the right to show/remarket the space to prospective new occupants is not tied to an actual notice of termination or a defined pre-expiration window (i.e., Landlord/Operator could market the space to replace Tenant at any point during an active term).
flag_if: Relocation clause with no requirement that Landlord bear all relocation costs (moving, reinstallation, signage, IT/telecom reconnection)
Relocation clause allows a move to space that is not expressly "substantially similar" in size, quality, or configuration, or omits any comparability standard entirely
Relocation notice period is silent or shorter than 60 days
No Tenant right to terminate or receive rent abatement if the substitute premises are unsuitable or the relocation disrupts business operations
Access/entry clause allows Landlord or Operator to enter "at any time" or "without notice" for non-emergency purposes
Access clause allows Landlord/Operator to show, market, or "resell" the space to prospective occupants without tying that right to an actual notice of termination or a defined pre-expiration window
Hybrid-working, shared-desk, or shared-use language with no defined maximum-occupancy cap or no stated enforcement mechanism for that cap

The reserved-rights or access language appears as a clause newly inserted late in negotiation with no counterpart in the original draft (before_text is blank/absent) — a sign the other side's counsel added it unilaterally and it may not have been substantively negotiated
preferred_language:
Landlord's Right to Relocate; Access to Premises.
(a) Relocation. Landlord shall have no right to relocate Tenant during the Term except as expressly set forth in this Section. Any relocation shall be undertaken entirely at Landlord's sole cost and expense (including, without limitation, all costs of moving, reinstallation, new signage, and reconnection of telecommunications, data, and other utilities), to substitute premises of substantially equal or greater size, and of comparable or superior quality, configuration, and location within the property, upon not less than ninety (90) days' prior written notice to Tenant. Tenant shall have the right, exercisable by written notice within thirty (30) days after receipt of Landlord's relocation notice, to terminate this Lease without penalty if Tenant reasonably determines the proposed substitute premises are not suitable for Tenant's business operations. Base Rent and other charges shall abate during any period Tenant is unable to occupy the Premises or the substitute premises as a result of the relocation.

(b) Access to Premises. Landlord and its authorized agents may enter the Premises only (i) in a genuine emergency threatening life, safety, or property, without prior notice; or (ii) for inspection, maintenance, or repairs, or to show the Premises to prospective purchasers or lenders at any time, or to prospective replacement tenants only during the last one hundred eighty (180) days of the Term or after Tenant has given notice of non-renewal or early termination, in each case upon not less than forty-eight (48) hours' prior written or electronic notice to Tenant and, if requested by Tenant, accompanied by a Tenant representative. All such entries shall be conducted so as to minimize interference with Tenant's business operations and shall comply with Tenant's reasonable security and confidentiality requirements. Any permitted hybrid-working, shared-desk, or shared-use arrangement shall at no time result in more individuals occupying the accommodation than the maximum occupant limit stated in this Agreement.
confidence_note: Based on only 2 findings, from two quite different real-estate contract types (a traditional ground-lease relocation clause with East End Maker Hub Sponsor and a flexible-workspace/coworking access-and-hybrid-working clause with IWG/Regus) and two different counterparties; both are "medium" significance and both show the counterparty's broad reserved-rights language being accepted into the final signed agreement with only baseline guardrails (landlord's-cost, size/quality comparability, notice period, occupancy cap) rather than being negotiated away or heavily contested — directionally consistent in outcome but thin in volume and heterogeneous in subject matter, so this rule should be treated as provisional and revisited as more findings accumulate.

title: Surrender / Return Condition & Post-Termination Survival
where_to_look: The "Surrender," "Return of Premises," or "Condition on Surrender" provision, typically near the end-of-term/expiration provisions or in a Default & End-of-Term section; also check the Alterations clause for any cross-referenced removal-at-surrender language, and check whether a Survival clause (often at the tail of the Surrender section or in Miscellaneous/General Provisions) caps how long these obligations continue post-termination.
required: Tenant's surrender obligation should require return of the Premises broom-clean and in good order, condition, and repair, subject to three carve-outs: (1) ordinary wear and tear, (2) damage from fire or other casualty (typically insured), and (3) any condition falling within Landlord's own repair/maintenance obligations under the lease. Removal of Tenant's alterations at surrender should be required only if Landlord gave Tenant written notice, at the time the alteration was installed/approved, that removal would be required at lease-end — no open-ended, after-the-fact removal demands. Obligations surviving expiration/termination under the Surrender section should be subject to a defined sunset (e.g., 6 months post-termination) rather than surviving indefinitely.
fallback: If the full package above isn't obtainable, prioritize (a) the casualty/insured-damage and landlord-maintenance carve-outs to the return-condition standard, and (b) some defined survival cap (even if longer than 6 months, e.g., 12 months) over the written-notice-at-installation requirement for alteration removal, which is the most frequently contested of the three elements.
escalate_if: Escalate to an attorney if the surrender obligations survive termination indefinitely with no stated end point AND the lease simultaneously gives the counterparty unfettered discretion to demand alteration removal at lease-end without any advance notice — that combination creates open-ended, unbounded post-termination liability. Also escalate if the return-condition standard would require Marmon to bear restoration or removal costs for casualty damage that is separately covered by insurance (risk of double-recovery/double-charge), or if a proposed survival period exceeds what's reasonable relative to the governing-law statute of limitations for contract claims.
flag_if: Surrender clause requires return 'broom-clean and in good condition' with no express ordinary-wear-and-tear exception
No carve-out from the return-condition standard for fire/casualty damage or for conditions that are the landlord's own repair/maintenance responsibility

Clause lets the landlord demand removal of tenant alterations 'at Landlord's option' or 'as Landlord may require' at surrender, with no requirement that removal be flagged in writing when the alteration was installed
Survival language states surrender obligations survive termination 'indefinitely' or contains no stated expiration/sunset for post-termination claims
No defined time window (e.g., a number of months) within which a claim under the surrender provision must be brought after lease-end
preferred_language: Surrender. Upon the expiration or earlier termination of this Lease, Tenant shall surrender the Premises to Landlord broom-clean and in good order, condition, and repair, reasonable wear and tear excepted, and further excepted for (a) damage caused by fire or other casualty, and (b) any condition that Landlord is obligated to repair or maintain under this Lease. Tenant shall be required to remove any alterations, additions, or improvements made by Tenant only if, at the time Landlord approved or was notified of such alteration, Landlord notified Tenant in writing that removal would be required upon surrender; absent such written notice given at that time, Tenant may leave the alteration in place at surrender without any removal or restoration obligation. The obligations of Tenant under this Section shall survive the expiration or earlier termination of this Lease, provided that any claim by Landlord arising under this Section must be asserted, if at all, within six (6) months after the date of such expiration or termination, after which time Tenant's obligations under this Section shall automatically terminate and be of no further force or effect.
confidence_note: Based on only 3 findings, and all 3 come from a single contract negotiation (one counterparty, Indiana Athletic Apparel, LLC, request 3807) rather than multiple independent deals; the direction is internally consistent within that one deal (each change reduces post-termination exposure — casualty/maintenance carve-out, advance-notice-for-removal, and a 6-month survival cap), but this is a thin, single-source sample, so treat this rule as provisional pending corroboration from additional Real Estate contracts before elevating its priority.
